statement: enforcer-config's EffectiveConfig::supported_platforms carries #[serde(default = "Platform::all")] so a genuinely ABSENT config field and an EXPLICIT ["windows","macos","linux"] declaration decode to the identical Vec<Platform> value — there is no way to recover which one happened from the decoded struct alone. PORT-1.1's workpack requirement ("no declaration + any platform-specific script fails (unchanged default)" vs. "declared [\"linux\"] only is NOT hard-failed for a Linux-only script") needs to distinguish exactly that case: an explicit full-platform declaration must relax fully, but a missing field must stay strict. Solved by NOT taking EffectiveConfig::supported_platforms directly into the validator; instead defined a local tri-state enum (DeclaredScope::{Declared(Vec<Platform>), Undeclared}) that the CALLER (whoever resolves the project's actual config source, before it flows through enforcer-config's total-struct default) must populate honestly.
why: A first implementation passed Vec<Platform> straight through and used Platform::all() as the 'no declaration' test input — the fixture-derived unit test (no_declaration_defaults_to_all_platforms_and_still_fails) failed left=0 right=1 because Platform::all() is indistinguishable from an explicit full declaration once inside the validator, so the 'strict unless narrowed' semantics silently became 'always relaxed for the all-three case'. This is a general trap: any total-struct config default that backfills an Option/missing-field to a non-empty value destroys the caller's ability to later special-case 'was this actually declared'.
howToApply: When a rule's spec requires different behavior for 'field absent (default applied)' vs 'field explicitly set to the same value as the default', do not thread the post-default value into the validator — thread a tri-state (declared vs not) resolved BEFORE the default is applied, or thread the pre-default Option<T> if the config crate can expose it. Grep any other RuleId whose spec says 'missing X defaults to Y, no silent relaxation by omission' (CFG-1, ENF-1 rows reference similar defaulting language) before assuming a config crate's total-struct default is safe to pass straight into a validator's decision logic.

evidence.ref: crates/enforcer-lang-common/src/port_platform.rs — no_declaration_is_unchanged_strict_default_and_still_fails test; see also explicit_all_three_platforms_declared_is_fully_relaxed which proves the two cases are now genuinely distinguishable

statement: rules/rules.json (workspace root, 569 total rules, 269 language==common) is NOT a bare JSON array — it is an envelope object { schemaVersion, productName, languages, rules: [...] }. Every rule entry uses id (not ruleId) and validator (a bare validator-id string like "common/architecture", not the enforcer-rules::registry::ValidatorRef {crateName,path} shape). This is the LEGACY .mjs-era catalog format; enforcer-rules's own Rust-native rules/*.json catalogs (deny-wall.json, no-reexports.json, ocentra-parent-posture.json) use a completely different, already-typed RuleRecord shape (ruleId/version/title/tier/validator{crateName,path}/fixtures{fail,pass}/docAnchor/tags/params). As of this lane (2026-07-04), NO enforcer-rules RuleRecord catalog exists yet for ANY of the 269 common-family rules, or the SEC-2/ts/py rows either — only 6 baseline T1 records (deny-wall x1, no-reexports x1, ocentra-parent-posture x4) have been ported to the new shape.
why: A workpack instruction like 'keyed to their RuleIds in enforcer-rules' or 'reads rules.json' can be misread as requiring either (a) writing new enforcer-rules/rules/*.json RuleRecord catalogs, or (b) reading the legacy envelope directly for a parity/count check. This lane deliberately chose (b) — direct legacy-JSON read via a crate-local minimal-decode struct in the test file — and left (a) undone as explicit follow-on scope, because writing 249 RuleRecord entries touches crates/enforcer-rules/rules/**, which is outside this workpack's owns: crates/enforcer-lang-common/** and would violate disjoint-owns with whichever pack (arc-04 follow-on, or a dedicated bridge pack) is meant to own that migration.
howToApply: Any future lane reading rules/rules.json for a count-parity or inventory check should decode the { rules: [...] } envelope, not a bare array, and use the legacy field names (id, validator as a string, language, severity, doc) — not the enforcer-rules RuleRecord field names. If a workpack seems to require enforcer-rules RuleRecord entries for a rule family that has none yet, treat that as a distinct, separately-claimable scope (touches crates/enforcer-rules/rules/**) and flag/spawn it rather than folding it into a lang-* crate's owns:.

evidence.ref: node -e require('./rules/rules.json') top-level keys = [languages, productName, rules, schemaVersion]; crates/enforcer-rules/rules/*.json (3 files, 6 total RuleRecords) vs 269 language==common entries in rules/rules.json with zero RuleRecord coverage

statement: The arc-09 workpack (docs/plans/enforcer-selfhost-plan/workpacks/arc-09-enforcer-lang-common.md) has zero corresponding rows in TEST_PROOF_EXPECTATIONS.md under its own name — grep for 'arc-09' and 'enforcer-lang-common' in that file only surfaces FIVE PRE-EXISTING rows (d03, d10, d16, d21, d23) that ALSO target `cargo test -p enforcer-lang-common` but for entirely different rule families (deferred-work-gate, resilience-auditor, fsm-transition, change-discipline, size-shape/test-quality) that do NOT appear anywhere in arc-09's own 30-prefix rule inventory table (ARCH-1, CI-1, PROOF-1, etc). Nothing in either document says whether those five D-track rule families are meant to live inside crates/enforcer-lang-common (making this crate a shared home for BOTH the arc-09 common-family rules AND the D-track review-heuristic rules) or whether that's a stale/aspirational reference to a crate name collision.
why: A worker executing arc-09 literally (owns: crates/enforcer-lang-common/**, do not read sibling workpacks) will build exactly the 249-rule count-parity set this pack specifies and correctly NOT touch d03/d10/d16/d21/d23's rule bodies (those are out of this pack's Rule inventory table) — but the crate will then look 'incomplete' to anyone reading TEST_PROOF_EXPECTATIONS.md expecting resilience-auditor/fsm-transition/etc. tests to exist here, because those rows predate or point past arc-09's actual scope.
howToApply: Before treating crates/enforcer-lang-common as 'done' project-wide, the orchestrator (not a single lane) should reconcile: either (a) the d03/d10/d16/d21/d23 workpacks also legitimately own slices of crates/enforcer-lang-common/src/ (in which case TEST_PROOF_EXPECTATIONS.md's existing rows are correct and arc-09 + those five D-track packs are co-owners of one crate, needing an explicit disjoint sub-ownership note), or (b) those five rows are stale and should be repointed at whatever crate the D-track rules actually landed/will land in. Do not add new arc-09-specific rows to TEST_PROOF_EXPECTATIONS.md from within this lane (outside owns: scope) — flag it for primary/orchestrator integration instead.

evidence.ref: grep -n -i 'arc-09|enforcer-lang-common' docs/plans/enforcer-selfhost-plan/TEST_PROOF_EXPECTATIONS.md -> only lines 183,190,196,199,200,201 (d03/d10/d16/d21/d23), zero arc-09-named rows
